Tiled: When Design Becomes a Learning Advantage

How an interactive microapp platform is transforming our curriculum—and why we're running an A/B test to prove that great design actually drives better learning outcomes.

I've spent months building the Future of PMM curriculum. Eight units. Dozens of pages. AI labs. Quizzes. The whole thing lives on a standard web stack—clean HTML, some JavaScript, hosted on Netlify. It works. People learn from it.

But last month, Anthony Brock from Tiled reached out with a question that made me pause: What if the content could feel different?

Not different information—the same curriculum. But wrapped in an experience designed to hold attention, guide the eye, and make the act of learning feel less like reading documentation and more like exploring something you actually want to explore.

The result is live now: s.tiled.co/2r9iip5/sap-curriculum

The personalized welcome screen with course navigation—a far cry from a static webpage.

It's the same Introduction and Unit 1 content. Same concepts. Same frameworks. But transformed into what Tiled calls a "microapp"—an interactive, animated, visually immersive experience that feels closer to a presentation than a webpage.

What Is Tiled, Exactly?

Tiled is an interactive content platform based in Utah, founded by Darrell Swain. The core idea: take your existing content—PowerPoints, PDFs, Figma designs—and transform them into shareable, trackable, interactive experiences without writing code.

They call these "microapps." Think of it as what happens when a presentation, a landing page, and an analytics dashboard have a baby. You get something that looks premium, behaves like an app, and tells you exactly how people engaged with it.

Tiled at a Glance

Founded Utah-based startup
Product Interactive microapp platform
Integrations Figma, Adobe XD, PowerPoint, Seismic
Customers IBM, Equinox, Sunrun, Compass

Their customer list tells the story. IBM reported a 250% increase in content engagement after switching sales materials to Tiled microapps. Compass Canteen saw a 19% lift in conversion rates. These aren't vanity metrics—they're measuring whether people actually do something after consuming the content.

Section 1 with integrated stats cards, callout boxes, and visual hierarchy that guides the eye.

The Person Behind Our Partnership

Anthony Brock is a Senior Manager on Tiled's expansion team, working out of Lehi, Utah. His background includes stints at Domo, Adobe, and Pluralsight—all companies that understand how enterprise content works (and doesn't work). He's the one who saw the Future of PMM curriculum and thought: this could be better if it felt better.

That instinct—that design and learning are inseparable—is what caught my attention. Most people in the enablement space treat content as a vessel. You pour information into it. The vessel itself doesn't matter. Anthony's pitch was different: the vessel is part of the message.

Why This Matters for PMM

Product marketers spend their lives thinking about how to present information. Positioning. Messaging. Packaging. We obsess over whether a slide deck tells a story or just dumps data. We know that how you say something changes what people hear.

But when it comes to our own learning and enablement? We often settle for PDFs. Static pages. The same formats we'd never accept for a customer-facing asset.

The Tiled version of Unit 1 forces a question: if great design drives engagement in sales content, why wouldn't it drive engagement in learning content?

The AI Impact Matrix—same data as our standard curriculum, but presented with tabbed navigation and key insights highlighted.

The A/B Test: Proving It Works

Here's where it gets interesting. We're not just going to assert that the Tiled experience is better—we're going to test it.

🧪 Our Experiment

Control: Standard futureofpmm.com curriculum (Intro + Unit 1)
Treatment: Tiled microapp version of the same content
Metrics: Completion rate, time on content, quiz scores, learner satisfaction (post-unit survey)
Reporting: Results published here in 4 weeks

We'll randomly assign new enrollees to one experience or the other, track their progress through the same assessment, and see if the design difference translates to a learning difference. If the Tiled version drives better outcomes, we'll have a conversation about rolling it out across the full curriculum. If it doesn't, we'll have learned something important about where design matters and where content is king.

Either way, we publish the results.
